It is live on the DeepSeek website, app and API . DeepSeek claims stronger scores, faster task completion and shorter outputs than the September V4.1-Flash release . The company calls it a Pareto improvement in performance and cost. Alongside it, DeepSeek opened its Search and Fetch APIs to every developer. For agent builders, that means a cheaper coding model plus a first-party web layer behind one API key. TL;aDR Size: 552B backbone parameters plus 196B Engram parameters. It activates 8B parameters per token in prefill and 16B in decode. Context is 1M tokens, with up to 384K output tokens. Runs on: DeepSeek API as deepseek-flash . September V4.1-Flash weights (763B parameters, FP8) are MIT-licensed on Hugging Face. Hardware requirements and 1017 weights: Not disclosed. Performance: Beats the previous V4.1-Flash on all 11 benchmarks DeepSeek reported, by 2.0 to 11.1 points. Best: 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1, above Claude Opus 5 (74.0) in DeepSeek’s table. Worst: 42.6 on HLE without tools, versus 56.3 for Claude Opus 5. What is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017? DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is an updated post-training checkpoint of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served through the deepseek-flash model name. The architecture details below come from the V4.1-Flash technical report . DeepSeek team states that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 uses reinforcement learning with self-feedback for end-to-end project work. Its examples run from game creation to 3D modeling. It is tuned for DeepSeek Harness , Tencent CodeBuddy and WorkBuddy. DeepSeek recommends DeepSeek Harness v0.2.1-rc.1 or later. How does the V4.1-Flash architecture work? V4.1-Flash is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 40 Transformer layers. They split into a 20-layer causal encoder and a 20-layer decoder. Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED): Decoder global KV is projected from the final encoder hidden states. This nearly halves prefill compute. Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2): Layers run in Full, Reindex or Reuse mode. They share main KV and indexer keys across layers. FP4 main KV cache: Global KV drops to 890 bytes per token, about 1/4 of V4-Flash. SWA Bounded Replay: Persistent KV cache shrinks to roughly 1/8 of V4-Flash. Reasoning effort: A 1 to 100 scalar. The API tiers low, high and max map to 50, 75 and 100. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 benchmarks All scores below are DeepSeek’s own figures . DeepSeek ran Terminal-Bench 4.0 in Claude Code and DeepSWE in Mini-SWE-V2. ZeroBench-main uses Pass@5. The 1017 checkpoint leads on DeepSWE, Automation-Bench, Agents’ Last Exam and Apex Bench. Claude Opus 5 still leads on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ProgramBench, NL2Repo and HLE. The Search API returns ranked web results for a query. The Fetch API returns a single page as Markdown. DeepSeek says its in-house engine serves hundreds of millions of requests daily. All weights are live on […] The post Meet Kyutai REKI: The 2.4B VLA Model Bringing Efficient Memory to Robot Manipulation appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Kyutai, with Inria and École des Ponts, has released REKI , a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) for robot manipulation. The REKI vision-language-action model is pretrained only on public data. It also carries a cheap memory of its recent past. On three out-of-distribution benchmarks, only models about twice its size beat it. All weights are live on Hugging Face today. TL;DR Size: 2.4B parameters (2.2B Qwen3.5-2B VLM + 0.2B flow-matching action expert). Memory covers the last 3 frames, 1 s apart. Runs on: Benchmarked on 1 NVIDIA H100. 21.8 ms per action chunk, compiled, from 2 cameras at 256×256. Weights ship in BF16. No quantized variants announced. Performance: Best among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin Clean2Rand. Best: 90.4% on LIBERO-Plus, the top score in Kyutai’s comparison. Worst: 38.4% on RoboCasa365, well behind Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (57.4%). What is REKI? REKI is a vision-language-action model from Kyutai that maps camera views and an instruction to robot actions. It pairs a Qwen3.5-2B backbone with a 200M-parameter action expert. The expert generates action chunks by flow matching, integrated in 10 Euler steps. Robot state and flow time enter through adaptive RMSNorm. Each robot state layout gets its own small state MLP. How does REKI’s memory work? Most VLAs act on the current frame alone. Prior memory methods feed past frames to the VLM, unroll training, or add modules. Each option adds cost. REKI places memory inside the action expert instead. Before each frame’s action tokens sit 32 learned register tokens . They cross-attend the encoded prompt and views of that frame. They also self-attend the registers of earlier frames. Registers never read action tokens. So they depend only on observations, not flow time or robot state. They are computed once per frame and cached in a rolling window. The cost is small, per the project page : Reading cached registers adds 0.1 ms to a 21.8 ms chunk. The cache uses about 2 MiB of GPU memory per past frame. Training packs a 3-frame window into 1 batched pass. Memory also fixes a failure mode. Without it, arms often oscillate between 2 poses. On RoboTwin, oscillating episodes fall from 18.6% to 4.1% with memory. Kyutai attributes this to perceptual aliasing. How does REKI perform on benchmarks? REKI is pretrained once, then finetuned separately per benchmark. Scores below come from the model card and project page. LIBERO-Plus: 90.4%, ahead of Qwen-RobotManip (89.0%) and π0.5 (85.7%). RoboTwin Clean2Rand: 65.8%, behind only Qwen-RobotManip (68.5%). RoboCasa365: 38.4%, ahead of RLDX-1 (36.0%) and Qwen-RobotManip (35.9%). LIBERO (4 suites): 97.6%. RoboTwin 2.0 Easy / Hard: 85.9% / 84.6%. Pretraining helps most out of distribution. It adds 13.8 points on Clean2Rand and 30.3 under clutter. Memory adds 1.5 points on LIBERO-Plus and 5.4 on RoboCasa365. How does REKI compare with other VLAs? Feature REKI ( Kyutai ) Qwen-RobotManip ( Qwen ) π0.5 ( Physical Intelligence ) ABot-M0 ( AMAP ) Total size 2.4B 4.7B ( per Kyutai ) 3.3B ( per Kyutai ) 4.6B ( per Kyutai ) VLM backbone Qwen3.5-2B Qwen3.5-4B Gemma-based Not disclosed Pretraining data Public only Open-source + human video Includes own robot data Open-source (UniACT) Memory 32 registers, 3 frames In-context variant None None LIBERO-Plus 90.4 89.0 85.7 ( Kyutai eval ) 80.5 RoboTwin Clean2Rand (mean) 65.8 68.5 63.8 55.7 RoboCasa365 38.4 35.9 16.9 Not disclosed H100 latency, compiled 21.8 ms Not disclosed 33.8 ms ( openpi, Kyutai ) 46.1 ms ( Kyutai ) Weights Open, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 Not released Open, Apache-2.0 repo Open, Apache-2.0 repo Notes: Clean2Rand means are computed from the 6 conditions in Table 5 of the Qwen-RobotManip report . The Qwen report lists π0.5 at 84.4 on LIBERO-Plus. What data was REKI trained on? The mixture holds 1.0B frames plus 12.2M vision-language samples. Real-robot teleoperation provides 639.8M frames, simulation 193.9M and egocentric human video 170.9M. Sources include DROID, BridgeData V2, AgiBot World, EgoDex and EgoVerse. Pretraining ran 200,000 steps on 32 H100 GPUs. Kyutai keeps each dataset’s native control convention rather than remapping actions. How do you deploy REKI? Six checkpoints are listed: the pretrained base plus finetunes for LIBERO, RoboTwin (2 variants), RoboCasa365 and RoboCasa-GR1. Real-robot deployment uses the LeRobot async-inference gRPC protocol. On a UR5 arm, REKI was finetuned for 3k steps (1 hour) on 50 demonstrations per task.
